clinicalPearls: A heredofamilial optic atrophy of early childhood combined with neurological signs, forming part of the optic atrophy plus spectrum
Bilateral optic atrophy presents in infancy or early childhood with reduced acuity, nystagmus and pallor of the discs
Neurological features include cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, pyramidal signs, peripheral neuropathy and variable learning difficulty
Historically autosomal recessive, but biallelic and severe OPA1 variants now overlap with the classic phenotype, blurring the boundary with DOA-plus
OPA3 mutations cause a related recessive optic atrophy with extrapyramidal features and 3-methylglutaconic aciduria (Costeff syndrome)
The optic atrophy is usually non-progressive after early childhood, whereas neurological disability may advance
Diagnosis integrates the ophthalmic findings with the neurological syndrome and confirmatory genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Behr syndrome describes early-onset optic atrophy accompanied by a broader neurodegenerative picture, and is now understood as a mitochondrial dysfunction disorder rather than a single entity. Severe or biallelic mutations in OPA1, as well as mutations in OPA3 and other genes, impair mitochondrial fusion and energy metabolism in retinal ganglion cells and central neurons. The resulting degeneration affects the optic nerves together with cerebellar, pyramidal and peripheral nerve pathways, producing the characteristic combination of visual loss and neurological signs. The metabolic burden explains the overlap with 3-methylglutaconic aciduria in OPA3-related disease.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary spastic paraplegia complicated by optic atrophy
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain to assess cerebellar and white matter involvement and exclude other causes
OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex
Urinary organic acids for 3-methylglutaconic aciduria when OPA3 disease is suspected
Nerve conduction studies for peripheral neuropathy
Genetic panel testing including OPA1, OPA3 and wider mitochondrial genes
redFlags: Rapidly progressive neurological deterioration requiring exclusion of a treatable metabolic disorder
Regression of developmental milestones suggesting an evolving encephalopathy
Marked systemic or cardiac involvement pointing to a broader mitochondrial syndrome
Acute visual decompensation warranting reassessment for an alternative cause
reference.prognosis: The optic atrophy tends to stabilise after early childhood, but overall outcome is dictated by the neurological burden, which ranges from mild ataxia to significant motor and cognitive disability.
pitfalls: Labelling the child with isolated optic atrophy and overlooking subtle neurological signs
Assuming autosomal recessive inheritance when a severe OPA1 variant is responsible
Missing OPA3-related 3-methylglutaconic aciduria by not checking urinary organic acids
Attributing neurological features to the visual impairment rather than a shared mitochondrial process
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Provide low-vision aids and visual rehabilitation for the optic atrophy, which tends to stabilise after early childhood
Manage spasticity with physiotherapy and antispasticity agents such as baclofen, and support gait and balance in cerebellar ataxia
Treat peripheral neuropathy symptomatically and provide orthoses and mobility aids
Screen for 3-methylglutaconic aciduria in OPA3-related (Costeff) disease and manage any metabolic derangement
Monitor visual and neurological function over time to guide supportive interventions
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across ophthalmology, neurology, physiotherapy and developmental or educational support
Offer genetic counselling and family testing, clarifying inheritance according to the causative gene (OPA1, OPA3 or wider mitochondrial genes)
